title: Stop Punishing Mothers for Doing Their Job
author: Martinko, Katherine
summary: Katherine Martinko revisits the case of Karyann Parkinson, a Virginia mother convicted of "contributing to the delinquency of a minor" after letting her five-year-old son walk half a mile alone to collect goose feathers. Martinko argues the prosecution rests entirely on hypothetical risk rather than any actual harm, and reflects a broader cultural drift in which "good" parenting has been redefined as constant risk-elimination rather than reasonable judgment. She marshals crime and abduction statistics to show childhood has never been statistically safer, contrasting society's alarm over unsupervised outdoor play with its tolerance of well-documented harms like excessive screen time. The piece closes with a call for parents to defend their own authority to judge their children's capabilities and to normalize independent, free-ranging childhood again.
points: Uses the Parkinson prosecution to show how a legal system can punish a parenting judgment that caused no actual harm.
Cites FBI and Let Grow data (1 in 720,000 stranger-abduction odds; falling murder rates) to argue childhood is safer than public fear suggests.
Argues 'good parenting' has been redefined as fearful, risk-eliminating parenting rather than reasonable, context-based judgment.
Calls on parents to actively defend their right to assess their own children's capability for independence.
quotes: Parkinson, who has three older kids and was eight months pregnant at the time, had gone for a bike ride with Sam earlier in the day. When they got home, she had to make lunch, but he wasn't ready to stay inside. He asked to go back for more feathers, and she said yes.

Officials pressed charges, and Parkinson (who gave birth a few weeks later) was eventually convicted of "contributing to the delinquency of a minor", given a six-month suspended jail sentence, and put on the state's child abuse and neglect registry for seven years, which she worries could affect her ability to pass an upcoming bar exam.

The chances of a child getting abducted by a stranger are one in 720,000 (via Let Grow) and account for less than 1% of missing-child cases in the U.S. Nonprofit Let Grow points out that you're five times more likely to have a conjoined twin.
It is a tragedy of our times that so-called "good" parenting has become synonymous with fearful parenting (though most parents don't want to label it as such).
We have to stand up for our right, as mothers and fathers, to assess our own children's unique levels of capability and to determine whether they can go places on their own.
